newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see U.S. corn, wheat ending stocks lower.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see U.S. corn, wheat ending stocks lower.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department will likely raise its estimate for corn feed usage in Friday's Supply and Demand Report but an expected cut in exports should keep ending stocks above 900 million bushels, analysts said.

"I think the government is going to have to hone in on the fact that our feed usage is clearly bigger than what the trade wants to believe," Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities, said. "We've got expansion going on" in the pork industry.
USDA in March put corn stocks at 959 million bushels. It will release April estimates for ending stocks on Friday at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.
Wheat stocks were expected to fall by roughly 20 million bushels from USDA's previous estimate for 474 million. Analysts pointed to stronger-than-expected export demand.

Analysts said an outbreak of foot and mouth disease that forced hog herd liquidation in Taiwan and forced that country to ban pork exports would cut Taiwan's need for corn imports by as much as 50 million bushels.
But U.S. pork producers planned to fill the void left by Taiwan's export ban and expansion in the U.S. industry will lead to larger domestic feed demand, analysts said.

"We'll see some reduction in (corn) exports because of the problems dealing with Taiwan, probably 40 million to 50 million (bushel) decline in the carryover stock here overall," said Jerry Gidel, analyst with Dean Witter. "We're still going to stay above 900 million."
Gidel said domestic feed usage also would rise due partly to the poor quality of last year's corn crop.
An unusually cool growing season led to high moisture levels and forced farmers to use more of the corn for livestock feed.
But industrial usage might see a decline due to cutbacks in ethanol production, Gidel said
"The ethanol demand has not rebounded like I'd like to see it," Gidel said
Many ethanol producers shut down operations last summer when corn prices soared to all-time highs and some have been slow getting back online, Gidel said.
Wheat stocks were expected to slip as the export pace outstripped USDA expectations, said Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney.
"I think there will be a modest upward revision on the export, maybe 15 to 20 (million bushels), and a corresponding downward revision in the stocks," Gustafson said.
USDA in the March Supply and Demand Report put wheat exports at 950 million bushels, down from an estimated 1.241 billion in the 1995-96 crop year.
But analysts said world demand has remained strong and buyers have turned to U.S. supplies even with large crops in Canada, Argentina and Australia.

A harsh winter put Canada out of contention briefly, the poor quality of Argentina's wheat turned some buyers away and Australia was temporarily out the market this year after they maxed out available stockpiles, sources noted.
"The exports are running ahead of (USDA expectation)," Dean Witter's Gidel said. "They may be 20 to 40 million bushels underestimated."
